stories.headline: Avalanche fall to Stars 3-2 in shootout after two goals disallowed at Ball Arena
stories.summary:
The Colorado Avalanche lost 3-2 to the Dallas Stars in a shootout Wednesday night at Ball Arena, after having two first-period goals disallowed following reviews. Roope Hintz scored in the fourth round of the shootout to decide the game. The Avalanche collected three of a possible four points from the back-to-back set against their rival.

Colorado's Jaden Schwartz had a goal erased on a successful Stars offside challenge, and Gabe Landeskog had one taken away after a league-initiated review determined he used a kicking motion. Landeskog did score at 4:55 of the second period, redirecting a pass from Nazem Kadri. Miro Heiskanen tied it for Dallas on a play set up by former Avalanche forward Mikko Rantanen, and Arttu Hyry put the Stars ahead with a shorthanded breakaway goal 80 seconds into the third period.

Brock Nelson tied the game midway through the third on a rebound. Goaltender Scott Wedgewood made 20 saves in his second start of the season. Coach Jared Bednar said he liked the team's third-period response but disagreed with the kicking-motion call.

stories.headline: Broncos host Super Bowl champion Seahawks on Thursday night with depleted secondary
stories.summary:
The Broncos face the Seattle Seahawks at 6:15 p.m. Thursday at Empower Field at Mile High. Denver has won 35 of the 58 games in the series, and the matchup comes on a short week after the team's third win of the season.

The Broncos will be without cornerback Pat Surtain and safety Talanoa Hufanga, their two best defensive backs. They will try to slow Seattle receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who is on pace to threaten the NFL single-season receiving yards record. Seattle's running game has declined since running back Kenneth Walker left in free agency for Kansas City.

Defensive coordinator Vance Joseph is expected to use disguised blitzes against quarterback Sam Darnold, who faces one of the league's highest third-down blitz rates and is prone to interceptions. Denver's own offense has struggled against similar pressure, and coach Sean Payton said it will continue if the team cannot beat it.

stories.headline: Ballot measure committees have spent $23 million in Colorado, finance data show
stories.summary:
Outside groups backing or opposing Colorado ballot measures have spent about $23 million through September, according to the latest campaign finance data. The total covers advertising and consultants, including the cost of gathering petition signatures.

The largest single check so far was $2 million from the Voter Trust Initiative, which backs Amendment 84 requiring a second form of identification for ballots, to the 76 Group, a firm headed by former Senate Minority Leader Josh Penry. Yes for Colorado Kids, which backs Proposition NN, has raised more than $5 million, including $3 million from the National Education Association. Proposition NN would let the state keep revenue above the TABOR cap.

Brighter Colorado has raised $2.6 million to oppose Proposition NN, and Don't Price Us Out, which opposes both NN and Amendment 87, has raised more than $1 million. Vote Yes on 83, which supports a constitutional right to hunt and fish, has raised nearly $1.9 million, while No Pollution in the Constitution, opposing Amendment 82, has raised $1.8 million.

stories.headline: Republicans outspend Democrats to block Colorado legislative supermajority
stories.summary:
Republicans have spent more than $1.6 million to defend a Douglas County state Senate district they have held for 15 years, in an apparent effort to prevent a Democratic supermajority at the Capitol. Democrats are one House seat and one Senate seat short of two-thirds control in both chambers, which would allow them to override vetoes and refer constitutional amendments to the ballot.

In competitive races in Pueblo, Highlands Ranch and Loveland, Republican super PACs had spent about $6.7 million as of Oct. 10, more than four times Democratic spending. In Senate District 30, Democratic groups had spent nothing against Sen. John Carson as of that date. The district covers Highlands Ranch, Castle Pines, Lone Tree and Roxborough Park.

A supermajority could weaken the next governor, likely Democratic Attorney General Phil Weiser, and force legislative Democrats to confront policy choices they have avoided with Gov. Jared Polis's veto as cover. Republican operative Daniel Cole called a Democratic supermajority the worst-case scenario.

stories.headline: Governor's Competitiveness Council releases 19 recommendations to boost Colorado business climate
stories.summary:
The Governor's Competitiveness Council, a public-private partnership led by Gov. Jared Polis, has released a policy roadmap aimed at making Colorado more competitive for business. The council was launched in July and held seven listening sessions statewide with more than 490 participants from 60 industries.

The roadmap lists 19 recommendations, including regulatory reforms, simplifying the sales and use tax system, expanding training incentives such as Opportunity Now and Skill Advance, and streamlining construction permitting. The University of Colorado's Leeds School of Business analyzed economic indicators for the effort.

According to the Colorado Chamber, the state ranks 38th nationally for cost of doing business, and the Metro Denver Economic Council ranked Colorado's 2025 employment growth 46th, down 30 spots from the prior year. Polis said he looks forward to reviewing the recommendations.

stories.headline: Denver releases draft plan to guide development around Burnham Yard
stories.summary:
The city of Denver has released a draft small area plan to guide development around Burnham Yard, the former rail yard site tied to the Broncos' stadium ambitions.

The city still needs to rezone the land, consider creating an urban renewal district on the site and complete environmental remediation before the project can break ground.

The Broncos, city leaders and Denver Water are also still working on an agreement to replace a large portion of the utility's campus, which sits within the Burnham Yard footprint.

stories.headline: Colorado housing slightly more affordable, national report finds
stories.summary:
Colorado saw a modest improvement in housing affordability, according to the National Housing Conference's report "Priced Out: When a good job isn't enough." Affordability improved by 1.98 percentage points for homeownership and 1.56 points for renters last year, the first homeownership gain in several years.

The report tracks 300 occupations in 390 metro areas to see whether average workers can spend 28% to 30% of income on housing. Only 4% of Colorado occupations can afford a home in their town, down from 13% in 2020, and 41% earn enough to rent a two-bedroom apartment, down from 50%.

Nineteen occupations, including dentists in Colorado Springs and sales managers in Greeley, gained enough in wages to afford a home with 10% down. Nationally, 14% of occupations can afford a home and 52% can afford to rent. Researcher Brittany Webb said Colorado remains unaffordable.

stories.headline: Man, 19, killed in I-70 crash with Colorado State Patrol vehicle east of Byers
stories.summary:
A 19-year-old man was killed and an 18-year-old driver seriously injured when their Ford F-150 crashed into a Colorado State Patrol vehicle and a tractor-trailer along Interstate 70 in Arapahoe County early Wednesday.

The crash happened at 6:45 a.m. as a trooper investigated a semitruck crash on westbound I-70 east of Byers. The patrol car was partially blocking the left lane while tow trucks removed the semi from the median. Investigators said the driver lost control, struck the patrol car, then hit a guardrail and the semi.

The passenger died at a hospital. The trooper was not injured but was taken to a hospital as a precaution. The Arapahoe County Coroner will release the victim's name, and the patrol's vehicular crimes unit is investigating.

stories.headline: Wrong-way I-25 driver had seven previous impaired driving charges, sheriff says
stories.summary:
William Dee Weitzel, 72, was arrested Tuesday after allegedly speeding the wrong way down southbound Interstate 25 near Castle Rock to evade deputies. Calls came in at 4:45 a.m. near Plum Creek Parkway, and he reportedly exceeded 80 mph.

Douglas County deputies forced his car off the road using a tactical vehicle intervention. Officials said he showed multiple signs of impairment and refused a blood alcohol test. The highway was closed near C-470 during the incident.

The Denver Post confirmed six prior DUI or impaired driving charges through court records, with a seventh in Larimer County in 1988. He pleaded guilty at least four times and has a suspended license. He is held on $75,000 bail and is due in court Monday.

stories.headline: Denver Police launch online Driver Exchange for minor crashes
stories.summary:
The Denver Police Department is launching an online Driver Exchange platform Thursday that lets drivers swap information after minor, non-injury crashes without waiting for an officer. Police say it is especially useful during weather-related crash alerts.

Officers will still respond if a vehicle is immobile, a driver lacks a license or registration, or impairment is suspected. Chief Ron Thomas said the program frees officers for urgent calls. The service is provided by Carfax for Police at no charge to the city or drivers, and is used by Longmont, Castle Rock, Montrose and Loveland.

Carfax obtains localized crash and registration data for its vehicle history reports. Privacy advocates have raised concerns that driver data is being commercialized in violation of the federal Driver's Privacy Protection Act.

stories.headline: LoDo neighbors urge Denver to crack down on unlicensed hot dog carts
stories.summary:
Business owners and residents in LoDo are asking Denver to act on unlicensed hot dog carts that crowd sidewalks near Coors Field on weekend nights. On a recent Saturday, more than 30 carts lined Blake, Market and Larimer streets by 11 p.m.

Critics cite unrefrigerated food, inconsistent sanitary practices, butane-heated trays that occasionally explode, and grease and trash left behind. Brad Manske, CEO of ViewHouse, said licensed businesses pay fees and taxes and expect the city to regulate those without licenses.

One vendor said she would get proper licenses if offered but could not afford the cost. Neighbors say the city's response has been muted, even as officials acknowledge the number of carts and safety hazards has grown over the past year.

stories.headline: Rain and mountain snow give way to Thursday night freeze watch for Denver metro
stories.summary:
A powerful storm is bringing rain to the Denver metro area and snow to the mountains into Thursday, with up to a foot possible in the high country. Showers are expected for the morning commute, with skies clearing from north to south by midday and highs in the low to mid 50s.

The Broncos-Seahawks game Thursday night at Empower Field will be chilly and windy, with temperatures in the low to mid 40s by the fourth quarter. A Freeze Watch is in effect for the Denver metro and Eastern Plains through 9 a.m. Friday, with widespread frost or a hard freeze possible.

Warmer weather returns for the weekend, with highs in the mid 70s Saturday and above-normal, mostly dry conditions into next week.

weather.notable: About 15 degrees below the average high for this time of year.

topStory.headline: Two Container Ships Sink Near Strait of Hormuz as Attacks on Shipping Surge; Iran Cites Naval Mine
topStory.summary:
Two vessels sank near the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday after being struck in what maritime monitors describe as the sharpest rise in attacks on shipping since the US-Israel war with Iran began on February 28. The Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride went down after an attack the previous day, and the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank hours later, having been hit by a projectile on September 23, according to International Maritime Organization data. All 21 crew members aboard the GFS Pride were safely evacuated, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said, and no injuries were reported.

Iran gave a different account of the GFS Pride sinking. State television quoted a statement from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps saying the ship, carrying about 2,500 containers, was on an "illegal and dangerous route" when it struck a naval mine and caught fire. The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said it had received reports of a container ship struck by an unknown projectile, and maritime security sources told Reuters the GFS Pride was hit by a projectile, raising questions about Tehran's explanation. The Singapore port authority called the attacks "unprovoked, unjustifiable, and a breach of international law." The vessel's UAE-based manager, GFS Ship Management FZE, could not be reached for comment.

UKMTO reported at least five incidents, including drone strikes, on tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area in the previous 48 hours, and six vessels were attacked on Sunday alone. A Financial Times analysis found 24 ships were hit in the two weeks to October 11, including three refined energy product tankers and two crude oil tankers. "There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate," one maritime security source said. Two senior Iranian officials said Tehran has begun using new tactics against vessels it considers in violation of its restrictions. Separately, Iran's Tasnim news agency reported three fishermen were injured when a fishing boat was hit by an unidentified drone near Sirik in Hormozgan province, describing it as a US drone attack; Iranian authorities have not officially confirmed who was responsible.

Before the war, roughly 125 to 140 large commercial vessels, including oil tankers, gas carriers and container ships, transited the 24-mile strait each day. Traffic effectively halted on February 28, when the United States and Israel launched coordinated airstrikes across Iran, and had appeared to be recovering in recent months. Iran has repeatedly warned ships not to pass without its approval, while the US military has been guiding vessels along a route nearer Oman's coast. The GFS Pride is the second vessel to sink since the war began, according to IMO data.

The escalation has pushed oil shipments through the strait sharply lower and carries political consequences in the United States. US fuel prices have risen by almost 70% since the war began, and the Republican party is bracing for losses in the November 3 midterm elections that will decide control of Congress. The Guardian reported the surge in attacks suggests Iran is seeking to fully close the waterway to undercut President Donald Trump's efforts to lower fuel prices, while the administration has sought to blame Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for higher costs. Whether the US escorts can sustain commercial traffic, and how insurers and shippers respond to the continued attacks, remain key questions.
